catalog_quote: Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic; it falls on the penultimate syllable, and shifts to the right when suffixes are added (for exceptions, see below). For example, [wañú.špa] 'dying' ... wañu.či.ri.naya.ju.či.špa] 'to cause to be desiring to cause to commit suicide' ... Stress may be used paralinguistically for semantic focus. Stress is placed on the root or suffix carrying the contrastive semantic load. ... In the more innovative dialects, there are some exceptions to stress placement. For example, [šamu.nú.n] /šamu.nú.n/ 'they are coming (Npo.)' [kaŋ.gá] /kan.ká/ 'and you? (Imb.)' [kay.pi.ráh] /kay.pi.rák/ 'still here? (Imb.)' ... The remaining suffixes are the independents /-ka/ 'topic' and /-rak/ 'still/yet/first' which generally take stress in interrogative constructions. [p.18: An acute accent indicates suprasegmental non-penultimate stress, e.g., waqrana 'a cow?'.] [Aschmann 2020 §4.1 p.20: phonetic* stress or accent is almost entirely predictable, falling in almost all cases on the penultimate (next to last) syllable, and does not need to be written. fn.23: There is one very small exception to this rule, in which the accent shifts to the final syllable on the last word in the sentence in some cases, but this does not negate the general fact that accent is not phonemic* in Quichua on individual words like it is in Spanish or English. p.39: Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic*, and always falls on the penultimate syllable.]
world_status: statement found in an open source

For example, [sámu.nú.n] 'they are coming (Npo.)', [kaŋ.gá] /kan.ká/ 'and you? (Imb.)', [kay.pi.ráh] /kay.pi.rák/ 'still here? (Imb.)' new_statements.citation: Carpenter, Lawrence Kidd. 1982. Ecuadorian Quichua: descriptive sketch and variation. PhD dissertation, University of Florida (Gainesville). xxiv+527 pp.
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (551 pp., text + page scan). I rendered pp.204-206 (printed pp.182-184) and read them: p.182 heading 'Suprasegmentals' / 'Stress': "Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic; it falls on the penultimate syllable, and shifts to the right when suffixes are added (for exceptions, see below). For example, [wañú.špa] 'dying'.. [wañu.či.ri.naya.ju.špa]" (stress mark moving rightward through the suffix chain). p.183: "Stress may be used paralinguistically for semantic focus. Stress is placed on the root or suffix carrying the contrastive semantic load.. In the more innovative dialects, there are some exceptions to stress placement. For example, [šamu.nú.n] /šamu.nú.n/ 'they are coming (Npo.)'" p.184:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable (non-phonemic) and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; as suffixes are added the stress moves rightward so that it stays penultimate in the full suffixed word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated about secondary stress (Carpenter's transcriptions mark only one stress per word). Aschmann 2020 likewise says nothing on secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) Paralinguistic/contrastive focus can place stress on the root or on a particular suffix; (ii) in 'more innovative dialects' certain suffixes attract final stress: Napo distributive /-nú-/, and the independent suffixes /-ka/ 'topic' and /-rak/ 'still' in interrogatives (Imbabura examples); transcription convention (p.~20) uses an acute for non-penultimate stress, e.g. interrogative wagraná 'a cow?'. Aschmann 2020 §4.1 fn.23 adds: accent may shift to the final syllable of the sentence-final word in some cases; Imbabura/Upper Napo phrase-terminator suffixes sometimes fall outside the stress domain; none of these exceptions is attributed specifically to Pichincha/Calderón.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (suffixed) phonological word; statement is for Ecuadorian Quichua generally, with the phonology chapter explicitly based on the non-central dialect group that includes Pichincha (Calderón, Cayambe, Guallabamba, Quinche, Checa, Puembo, Tumbaco, Sangolquí were field sites), though Carpenter notes most chapter data come from Imbabura, Cañar, Loja and Napo. Corroborated for 'Pichincha / Salcedo (= Calderón) Quichua' among all Ecuadorian varieties by Aschmann 2020 §4.1 p.20 ('falling in almost all cases on the penultimate syllable') and pp.39-40 ('Stress in Quichua is non-phonemic, and always falls on the penultimate syllable'), and historically by Grimm 1896 p.1 ('Las palabras quichuas se acentúan ordinariamente en la penúltima sílaba').
new_statements.identity_note: No source found is devoted to Calderón (Pichincha) Quichua alone. Carpenter 1982 is a pan-Ecuadorian-Quichua dissertation whose phonology chapter is explicitly based on the 'non-central' dialect group that includes Pichincha (Calderón, Cayambe and six other Pichincha field sites) alongside Imbabura (imba1240), Cañar (cana1260), Loja (loja1240), S. Chimborazo and Napo; the stress rule is stated for all of them with dialect-specific exceptions only for Imbabura and Napo. Aschmann 2020 names 'Pichincha / Salcedo Quichua, also known as Calderón Quichua' as one of the varieties covered and states the same rule for all Ecuadorian Quichua. Glottolog's cald1236 phonology reference (Kohlberger 2010) actually describes Cotopaxi (Tigua) Quichua. Grimm 1896 describes Quito-area highland Quichua generally.

new_statements.quote: p.10: "Obsérvese que la penúltima sílaba -na-, ejemplos 2 y 3, que tiene acento prosódico, pasa a ser parte de Pastaza y Tena, y el acento debe ser escrito. En el ejemplo 4, el acento se queda en la sílaba -nga-, aunque en Tena ha perdido la última sílaba, y debe ser escrito." p.7: "la pérdida de la consonante del morfema añadido hace que el acento caiga en la sílaba final en los dialectos Pastaza y Tena." p.9: "Otra característica del dialecto Tena es que en los verbos de la tercera persona del presente de indicativo, se acentúa la sílaba final: pichán 'él (o ella) limpia, barre', shamún 'él (o ella) viene', micún 'él (o ella) come'."
new_statements.translation: p.10: "Note that the penultimate syllable -na-, examples 2 and 3, which carries the prosodic [default, unwritten] accent, becomes part of Pastaza and Tena, and the accent must be written. In example 4 the accent stays on the syllable -nga-, although in Tena the last syllable has been lost, and it must be written." p.7: "the loss of the consonant of the added morpheme makes the accent fall on the final syllable in the Pastaza and Tena dialects." p.9: "Another characteristic of the Tena dialect is that in third-person present indicative verbs the final syllable is stressed: pichán 's/he cleans, sweeps', shamún 's/he comes', micún 's/he eats'."
new_statements.citation: Orr, Carolyn. 1978. Dialectos quichuas del Ecuador con respecto a la preparación de materiales de lectura. Cuadernos Etnolingüísticos 2. Quito: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 86 pp.
new_statements.locator: p.10 (p.12), paragraph on Cuadro IV (Oriente dialects: Pastaza/Tena/Napo past-tense morphemes); supporting remarks p.7 (p.9), p.9 (p.11), p.23 (p.25). All verified against the page scan.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the saved the Internet Archive PDF (the PDF's metadata: 49 pp., LuraDocument 2009 scan, image-only) and the scanned; title page (p.3) reads 'DIALECTOS QUICHUAS DEL ECUADOR / Con respecto a Lectores Principiantes / Carolyn Orr D. / Instituto Linguistico de Verano.. Cuadernos Etnolinguisticos N.2 / Quito, Ecuador 1978' -- correct work. I rendered pp.11, 12, 13 at 110 dpi and read the page scan. p.10 (p.12) printed text: 'Observese que la penultima silaba -na-, ejemplos 2 y 3, que tiene acento prosodico, pasa a ser parte de Pastaza y Tena, y el acento debe ser escrito. En el ejemplo 4, el acento se queda en la silaba -nga-, aunque en Tena ha perdido la ultima silaba, y debe ser escrito.…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's penultimate record (Carpenter 1982) but only implicitly: Orr takes penultimate 'acento prosódico' as the unmarked default and marks accent only when it becomes final. Her explicit final-accent cases concern the Oriente dialects Pastaza and Tena (cf. Carpenter's and Aschmann's notes on Napo/lowland final stress after consonant loss), not the Pichincha/Calderón variety of this catalog entry, for which the work gives no accent statement. Adds nothing on Pichincha beyond consistency with the penultimate default.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No explicit stress rule is stated anywhere in the work (it is a segmental/morphemic dialect survey for preparing literacy primers). The accent remarks presuppose the pan-Ecuadorian-Quichua default: the penultimate syllable carries the 'acento prosódico' and needs no written mark; a written accent is required only where a dialect (Pastaza, Tena) has lost a final consonant or syllable so that the accent ends up word-final (sachái, picháun, rinaín, micunáin; Tena 3sg present pichán, shamún, micún). Spanish loans are re-accented to fit Quichua structure, the examples all landing on the penult: pajáru (Azuay), sabáru, albúru (Loja) (p.23). Nothing is said about accent in the Pichincha dialect specifically; Pichincha appears only in the Sierra segmental comparisons (sh for ch before consonants, l/ll distribution, vowel changes -mun/-munda, patbaj, etc.).
new_statements.exceptions: Final accent in Pastaza and Tena where a suffix consonant or final syllable has been lost (locative sachái, progressive picháun; Tena desiderative rinaín, micunáin; Pastaza/Tena past-tense forms of Cuadro IV), and in Tena 3rd-person-singular present indicative verbs (pichán, shamún, micún); these are Oriente dialects, not Pichincha. Loanword re-accentuation (pajáru, sabáru, albúru).
new_statements.identity_note: Orr 1978 is a survey of nine Ecuadorian Quichua dialect areas (Oriente: Pastaza, Tena, Napo; Sierra: Imbabura, Pichincha, Tungurahua, Chimborazo, Azuay, Loja). Pichincha (the province containing the Calderón field site of cald1236) figures only in the segmental/morphemic comparisons and the appendix wordlist; every accent remark in the work is about Pastaza/Tena (Oriente) or about Spanish loans in Azuay/Loja.

sources.quote: Quichua word accent is very regular, falling as a general rule on the penult (second-last syllable) of each word. In the following examples, the accented syllable of each word is capitalized: aLLIlla, alliLLAchu, CANgui, Ari. Sometimes, for added emphasis, the accent is shifted to the final syllable of a word. This is indicated by the use of a written accent mark over the accented syllable.
